Abjure
ăb-jūr´
v. (to renounce upon oath; to deny or disavow with a solemn asseveration)
Latin abjurare, to deny on oath, from ab-, away, and jurare, to swear. The word belongs to the persecutions: an accused Christian was required to abjure, and the formula was usually short.

Biblical Definition

To abjure is to renounce under oath. Peter did it: “And again he denied with an oath, I do not know the man” (Mat 26:72). The Lord states what hangs on it: “whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:33); and Paul repeats it: “if we deny him, he also will deny us” (2Ti 2:12). The apostles' refusal before the council is the counter-formula: “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye. For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:19–20). And the church at Pergamos is commended for holding fast: “hast not denied my faith, even in those days wherein Antipas was my faithful martyr” (Rev 2:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines abjure as to renounce upon oath; to abandon; and, in a general sense, to reject with solemnity; to renounce or reject with abhorrence.

expand to see more

ABJURE, v.t. To renounce upon oath; to abandon.

2. To renounce, discard or deny.

ABJURATION, n. The act of abjuring; a renunciation upon oath; as, an abjuration of the realm, by which a person swears to leave the country forever.

2. A rejection or denial with solemnity; a total abandonment.

Key Scripture

Mat 26:72 — "And again he denied with an oath, I do not know the man."

Mat 10:33 — "But whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven."

2Ti 2:12 — "If we suffer, we shall also reign with him: if we deny him, he also will deny us:"

Act 4:19 — "But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye."

Rev 2:13 — "I know thy works, and where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is: and thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith, even in those days wherein Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you, where Satan dwelleth."

Modern Corruption

Denial is imagined as a decision made under torture, and Peter's was made by a fire, to a servant girl.

expand to see more

The circumstances of the most famous denial in history are worth holding in view whenever a Christian wonders how he would do under persecution. Peter was not before a tribunal. He was warming himself at a fire in a courtyard, and the person who identified him was a maid. There was no torture, no formal charge, and no immediate threat of death — and this was a man who a few hours earlier had drawn a sword against an armed party and meant it. Courage in a crisis and courage in a conversation are not the same faculty, and the second fails more often.

The passage that terrifies is Matthew 10:33, and it must be read with the case beside it. Peter denied Christ three times, with an oath and with cursing, and was restored by name at a fire on a beach with a threefold question — and preached at Pentecost. So the warning cannot mean that a single failure is final; the Gospel that records the warning also records the restoration. What Matthew 10 describes is a settled disowning rather than a collapse repented of, and the difference between Peter and Judas is not the size of the sin but where each took it afterwards.

Revelation 2:13 gives the commendation in the language of ordinary faithfulness under real pressure: thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith, even in those days wherein Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you. The church at Pergamos had watched a man die and had gone on confessing. Nothing in the verse suggests they found it easy or that they were remarkable in any other respect — the same letter has hard things to say to them. They simply did not abjure, and the Lord names it first.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek arneomai (G720), to deny, disown; aparneomai (G533), to deny utterly; homologeo (G3670), to confess; krateo (G2902), to hold fast.

expand to see more

Greek arneomai (G720) — to deny, disown; Matthew 26:70–72, 10:33, 2 Timothy 2:12, Titus 1:16.

Greek homologeo (G3670) — to confess, say the same thing; Matthew 10:32, Romans 10:9, 1 John 1:9.

Greek krateo (G2902) — to hold fast; Revelation 2:13, 2:25, 3:11, Hebrews 4:14.

Usage

"“He denied with an oath” — by a fire, to a servant girl."

"“We cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” — the counter-formula."

"“Hast not denied my faith” — and they had watched Antipas die."
